1:
Gill fixes the moment: the word came immediately after the execution of Achan, the fierceness of God's anger being turned away. Henry makes that the whole point of the encouragement. Joshua was at a stand, not yet recovered from the trouble Achan had given him, and could not think of pushing forward without fear that there might be another Achan in the camp. Corruptions within the church, Henry observes, weaken the hands of her guides more than oppositions from without, and treacherous Israelites are more to be dreaded than malicious Canaanites. His rule follows: when we have faithfully put away the accursed thing that separates between us and God, then, and not till then, may we expect to hear from God to our comfort. Clarke says the same more briefly, the iniquity being purged. Ellicott hears in the words the return of Jehovah to the host for the prosecution of the war, and Calvin the deliberate raising of courage in men lately repulsed with disgrace.

The spoil is the second encouragement. Henry sets the two cases side by side: Achan, who caught at forbidden spoil, lost that and life and all, while the people who had refrained were quickly recompensed with the spoil of Ai. The way to have the comfort of what God allows, he concludes, is to forbear what he forbids. Ellicott is careful about the extent of the grant: the material spoil and the cattle, not the persons, Jericho having been the exceptional case in which the goods themselves were devoted as accursed. Wesley reads the order to take all the people as giving every man a share in this first spoil, though the weak multitude were left behind lest they hinder the stratagem, those who ran the hazard deserving precedency in the plunder. Calvin takes the spoils to be left them frankly as the reward of victory, and the burning of the city as a concession to popular feeling that wiped out the memory of their disgrace.

How many men went is disputed. Henry finds in the command to take all the people a tacit rebuke for the small detachment sent the first time, and Ellicott glosses it as more than the two or three thousand of the earlier attempt. Keil and Delitzsch read it more widely still: the instruction looked beyond Ai to the conquest of the whole land, not to be attempted by detachments but with the entire force. Clarke argues at length against all of this. Only thirty thousand were employed, the rest standing ready; it would have been absurd to march hundreds of thousands against a place whose whole population was twelve thousand, and the spies had judged three thousand enough. Having no battering-rams, Joshua used the feigned flight to draw the inhabitants out — whereas a larger force before the walls would have kept them safely inside and defeated the design.

Calvin explains the stratagem by the state of the men rather than the size of the town. Their hearts had melted, and God laid no greater burden on them than they could bear until the panic passed; he used their own exertion partly that they might not always be looking for miracles, and partly that under unequal modes of acting they might still recognise his power as the same. Henry doubts Joshua would have thought of an ambush unaided, and draws the application: though we are not to expect visions now, when men entrusted with public counsels take prudent measures it must be acknowledged that God puts it into their hearts. Ellicott closes with the name. Ai means the heap, so that when Joshua afterwards made it a heap for ever its first and last names agree; and while Palestine is full of Tels with some further name attached, the et-Tel by Bethel is simply the heap, which he thinks nearly enough to fix the site.
3:
Henry begins by defending the stratagem, since God himself appointed it and the like is therefore lawful in other wars. No league was broken — truth, once plighted, becomes a debt even to an enemy — and no untruth was told: nothing was concealed but their own counsels, which no enemy pretends a right to be entrusted with, and nothing counterfeited but a retreat, which is no indication of inability to renew the onset. The men of Ai ought to have kept within their walls, and common prudence would have forbidden them to pursue a superior army and leave their city unguarded; if they would be so easily imposed upon, Israel is not to be blamed for taking the advantage. Henry later turns the device upon Christ, of whom he takes Joshua for a type: Joshua conquered by yielding, as though himself beaten, and so our Lord in bowing his head seemed routed by death but rallied in his resurrection, breaking the serpent's head by suffering him to bruise his heel.

The numbers are the hard part. Thirty thousand are chosen and sent away by night, yet later it is five thousand who lie in ambush and enter the city. Henry lays out the options: some hold that two parties went out, thirty thousand first and five thousand afterwards to guard the roads, Joshua attacking with all the thousands of Israel — Bishop Patrick's view, resting on the command to take all the people; others that the whole host only encamped before the city, that thirty thousand were chosen from it for the action, and that five thousand were detached to lie in wait, as many as could march unseen before a larger body would be discovered and the design broken. Henry decides for a single ambush of five thousand, enough for the purpose, and accepts a seeming disturbance in the order of the narrative to get it. Wesley reaches the same conclusion more briskly: there are only two parties and one ambush, as appears from comparing the sending out with the later notice of five thousand, who must be part of the thirty thousand named. He also reads the opening words as meaning that Joshua and his council considered the expedition, not that all the people marched.

Ellicott admits the question cannot be answered with certainty, and shifts it to Joshua's object. He meant to isolate Ai, taking it in front and in flank; but another town lay less than two miles behind it, so a body large enough to close the communications between Bethel and Ai had to be employed from the first. Keil and Delitzsch supply the march: about fifteen miles from Gilgal by a north-westerly road, so that a detachment sent off at night could reach the western side of Ai before daybreak — Joshua meanwhile approaching with the rest and fleeing, if the garrison came out as before, until he had drawn them quite away. Gill fills in the signal, the watch set to see Israel flee and the men of Ai drawn far enough from the city.

Clarke raises a practical objection to the order about firing the city. It probably means no more than kindling a fire whose smoke would show the place was taken; for the spoil was to be divided among the people, and burning the city outright would have consumed everything, the five thousand having stayed to save nothing but issued out at once against the enemy's rear. Ellicott notes that the word here for the lurking-place is not the word used elsewhere for the ambush, and that Joshua lodged that night among the host at Gilgal. Henry ends on their obedience: the men posted between two confederate cities stood in real danger and might have been cut off, yet they went; and the retreat ordered of the main body was disgraceful and perilous, yet they did it without murmuring.
10:
Gill has Joshua rise early and number the people. Clarke reads the verb as inspecting the ranks, and adds that had the whole force been shown, the men of Ai would never have risked a battle but kept safely within their walls, which was the one thing Joshua had to prevent. Wesley agrees that it was not all Israel who were counted but the remainder of the thirty thousand, mustered to see whether any had slipped away in the night. Keil and Delitzsch place the camp north of Ai with the valley between; Ellicott identifies the ravine north of et-Tel and puts the main body on the rising ground beyond it. The wider valley Joshua entered that night, Ellicott adds, was chosen to draw the garrison into a pursuit down the Gilgal road.

The five thousand raise the old question again. Gill follows the rabbis in making this a second ambush, perhaps set nearer the city. Wesley reads the verb as a pluperfect, the notice being a recapitulation rather than a new detachment. Calvin doubts the whole host was called out at all, and takes the thirty-five thousand who seem to be enumerated as a distribution rather than a sum: thirty thousand for the open fight and five thousand for the ambush, since it would be pointless to reinforce so great a multitude with so small a body, and the place named is the same in both notices. Ellicott, having studied the ground on the Ordnance map, comes down the other way: two ravines come to a head between Bethel and Ai, the firing party lying in the nearer one and the larger body, whose business was to prevent interference from Bethel, in the ravine next that city.

Calvin is blunt on the propriety of the device: the question whether it is lawful to overcome an enemy by wiles originates in gross ignorance, since the best commanders accomplish more by art and counsel than by violence, and if war is lawful at all then the usual methods of conquering are lawful, provided only that faith once pledged is not violated.

Ellicott thinks the feint worked because Joshua gave the enemy time in open daylight to read his apparent intention of renewing the direct assault; they came out meaning to drive him back the way he had come, and he fled in exactly that direction. Wesley notes the appointed hour agreed between Ai and Bethel, and guesses they may have chosen the same hour at which they had beaten Israel before, reckoning it lucky. Keil and Delitzsch observe that not one soldier was left in either town, Bethel having probably come in under a treaty. Gill raises the difficulty of how the Bethelites joined with the ambush lying between the towns, and answers that they either went round or were let through on purpose, so that Bethel too might be emptied.

The spear is disputed. Gill and Clarke both suppose a flag or ensign on it, unfurled as the sign agreed upon; Keil and Delitzsch think it would have been visible at a good distance even without one, since Joshua would have taken his station on some eminence rather than among the flying men. Calvin doubts it could have been seen from the ambush across that space, and from a valley at that, and suggests the men may have risen of their own accord on hearing the battle joined — while insisting the raised spear was in any case a badge of assured victory. Ellicott sets it beside Jericho: there the hand of Jehovah alone did the work, here the hand of Israel and first of all the hand of Joshua, stretched out as Moses stretched the rod over Amalek. Calvin and Wesley agree that the fire kindled was partial, enough to signal the capture, since it would have been absurd to burn the spoil God had granted.
23:
Henry states the ground first: God the righteous Judge had passed sentence on the Canaanites for their wickedness, so that Israel were only the ministers of his justice. He notes that the men of Bethel threw themselves into Ai as the stronger place and were cut off with it, so that what they hoped would prevent their ruin hastened it; and that those whom God will destroy he first infatuates. Clarke takes the smiting of the city to refer to the women, children and old men left behind, every effective man having sallied out. Calvin reads the total the other way: not that all the slain belonged to Ai but that all who dwelt there were slain, none escaping; and though he will not dispute with those who confine the number to the town, he thinks it likelier that it takes in those who fell in the field.

The outstretched spear draws more comment than the battle. Clarke insists on a plain sense: Joshua was not only the general but the standard-bearer of his own army, and though some read the gesture as continued prayer, he cannot think it carries the meaning found in the lifting of Moses' hands. Keil and Delitzsch explain it by the custom of war, that a general does not lower the signal until the conflict is to cease; Wesley makes it a sign to encourage and direct. Henry finds self-denial in it: the fire of courage would have carried Joshua sword in hand into the action, and in obedience to God he kept instead the inferior post of standard-bearer, directing the people to expect their help from God. Calvin puts it more strongly: it was as if Joshua had resigned the office of leader and transferred the whole praise to God, standing aloof with his hand as it were fastened to the spear.

On the spoil they are brief. Ellicott and Clarke both mark the contrast with Jericho, whose spoil had been claimed for Jehovah alone while this was assigned to Israel. Henry adds that the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just, and supposes the plunder was collected and distributed in due proportions rather than seized by violence, since God is the God of order and not of confusion. Gill points out that the whole city was now burnt, the earlier fire having been set to a few houses for a signal. Ellicott gives the Hebrew of the heap for ever and its modern name, and Henry notes that the place seems never to have been rebuilt.

Gill and Wesley agree the king was taken alive and reserved for a more ignominious death. Wesley explains the severity: the kings were dealt with harder because the people's wickedness had been countenanced by their example, and they were the chief authors of their nation's destruction. Calvin argues the same: conquerors usually spare captive kings, but here vengeance fell sternest on the leaders, and God delivered this one alive that his punishment might be the more marked. Clarke supposes he was strangled before being hung, since it was not then customary to hang men alive, and passes on the Greek reading of a double or forked tree. Keil and Delitzsch record that the body came down at sunset in obedience to the law, was cast at the gate, and had stones piled on it as Achan had; Calvin takes the burial as proof that nothing was done in tumult. Henry and Wesley both notice that the gate was where the king had sat in judgment, so that he was punished where he had made his unrighteous decrees. Ellicott asks why the text says the tree, guesses the king of Jericho may have hung on the same one, and turns to the greater Joshua, who fulfilled the curse of God in his own person and triumphed over principalities and powers in his cross.
30:
The ceremony comes in surprisingly, as Henry says, mid-war: the camp is drawn out not to engage an enemy but to sacrifice, hear the law read and say Amen. Whether it stands in its right place is disputed. Calvin presses it hardest: one verse closes the destruction of Ai and the next opens abruptly with an altar twenty miles off, and the march of the whole body through hostile country must have cost time and labour, yet not a word is said of it. He concludes that the order of time has not been observed, treats the passage as an episode belonging later, and notes that the Greek gives it after the league of the Amorites. Ellicott answers that the opening word is a note of time and not a mere connective, and that there is no reason to move it: the capture of Ai had given Joshua command of the road to Shechem, and no strong place lay north of Bethel. Henry likewise refuses a transposition; Keil and Delitzsch add that after Ai, Israel had a footing firm enough for the instructions of the law to be carried out. Wesley denies that the command required it on the day of the crossing, since circumcision and the passover came first; Gill reports that the Jews think otherwise, and are obliged to march Israel a hundred and twenty miles in a day.

Henry makes much of its standing on Ebal, the mount of the curse: there, where by the law we had reason to expect a curse, we have peace through Christ, who was made a curse for us. Wesley draws the same inference from the site. On the unhewn stones Calvin is sharp with the allegorists: it is true and wise that our own devices vitiate worship, but out of place here, since the intention was simply to prevent altars from becoming permanent. Henry takes the rough stone to mean that God is best pleased with what is plain and natural in worship.

What was written on the plastered stones nobody thinks was the whole law. Clarke renders the phrase the repetition of the law and confines it to the blessings and curses of the occasion. Gill lists the options — an abstract of the laws, the decalogue, or the blessings and curses. Wesley asks what stones and what time would have sufficed for the five books, and settles on the weightiest parts. Calvin agrees that no stones could contain the details and takes it for the substance and sanctions only: strangers entering the land could see at once what God was worshipped there, for though the priests should have been dumb the stones themselves spoke clearly. Henry observes that this copy was written on plaster and not graven as the tables in the ark were, since to write the law in the heart is God's prerogative.

Henry notes that the elders and judges were not above the law's cognizance, and the poorest stranger was effectively naturalised — a presage of kindness to the Gentiles. Every word was read, and the women and little ones were present, from which he concludes that masters of families should bring their households to solemn assemblies. Clarke gives a further reason for the women's presence: the education of the children was chiefly entrusted to them. Calvin describes the arrangement — six tribes on either mount with the ark between, so that the Lord was surrounded by his own people — and dwells on the order of blessing and cursing: Joshua blessed first, since God's purpose was to allure by sweetness, the curses being added when invitation proved unavailing; and by answering Amen to every sentence each man became his own herald, denouncing the punishment that would await him. Ellicott ends with a practical note: that the law could be read from this position and heard by the whole congregation has been proved by experiment.
